title: Direct identification through registration details shared by the homeowner
description: During account registration and device enrollment, the homeowner may provide directly identifying data such as name, email address, phone number, account username, home address, or device ownership details. The act of sharing this data with the Home Hub can identify the individual behind the smart-home deployment.
assumptions: Assumes registration involves personal account details rather than fully anonymous local-only setup.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort based on general LINDDUN identification categorization; exact sub-node may differ in the full threat tree.

title: Linkability of multiple devices and sensors to the same homeowner
description: By enrolling multiple cameras and sensors in one registration/enrollment action, the homeowner causes several device identifiers, serial numbers, and capabilities to become associated with the same account or person. This can enable linking of separate devices and activities to one household or individual.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub binds enrolled devices to a single account, household profile, or owner identity.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree sub-node may vary; grounded in general linkability of records and identifiers.

title: Identification via data in transit during registration and enrollment
description: If registration and enrollment data traverse the flow without strong protection, personal details and device identifiers in transit could reveal the homeowner's identity or household identity to observers on the local network or adjacent infrastructure.
assumptions: Assumes the flow may traverse a network where eavesdropping is possible and transport protections may be absent or weak.
uncertainty_note: Applies primarily when transport confidentiality/integrity protections are insufficient.

title: Linkability through enrollment metadata on the flow
description: Even aside from payload contents, metadata on the registration/enrollment flow—such as timing, source endpoint, repeated pairing attempts, and sets of device identifiers—may allow an observer to link multiple devices and setup events to the same household.
assumptions: Assumes observable communication metadata exists on the network or intermediary path.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is approximate; this is a metadata-based linkability threat at the flow.

title: Detectability of home occupancy and device presence by the Home Hub
description: On receipt of registration and enrollment data, the Home Hub learns that a specific home contains cameras and sensors and can detect the presence, type, and number of monitoring devices associated with that household. This makes the existence of the homeowner's smart-home setup detectable to the recipient.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub stores or processes enrollment details in a way that exposes device presence within the system context.
uncertainty_note: Exact detectability sub-node is approximate; threat is that the recipient can observe the existence/presence of the subject's devices and setup.

title: Unawareness of how registration and enrollment data will be used
description: The Home Hub may collect account details and device metadata during setup without making it sufficiently clear to the homeowner how this information will be stored, combined, retained, or used for later analytics, remote access, support, or feature enablement. The privacy threat arises at the destination because the recipient's processing may not be transparent to the user.
assumptions: Assumes setup UX or notices may be incomplete or unclear regarding downstream processing.
uncertainty_note: This is a common destination-side unawareness threat, but applicability depends on the actual notice/consent design.

title: Non-compliance risk from excessive collection during onboarding
description: The Home Hub may receive more personal data and device metadata than necessary for basic account creation and device enrollment, such as unnecessary profile attributes or overly detailed device information. If so, the recipient's collection and processing could violate data minimization, purpose limitation, or transparency obligations.
assumptions: Assumes onboarding may request or retain data beyond what is strictly necessary for setup.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and product context; exact sub-node is approximate.

title: Guest may be unaware they are sharing personal data when entering the temporary access code
description: When the guest enters the temporary access code at the Home Hub, they may not realize the code entry can be treated as personal data about them or linked to their visit, especially if the hub logs code use together with time and door-unlock events.
assumptions: Assumes the temporary code is associated with a specific guest, invitation, or visit window, or that the event can otherwise be tied to an identifiable person.

title: Code-entry transmission metadata may enable linking of guest visits
description: Even if the temporary access code itself is short-lived, the transmission on this flow can reveal metadata such as when a guest attempted entry and which hub received the code. Repeated observations could link multiple access events to the same guest or household visit pattern.
assumptions: Assumes an observer can access or infer communication metadata on this flow, for example via local network, device telemetry, or side-channel observation.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement because the retrieved context did not include the detailed linkability subtree.

title: Home Hub may identify the guest from the temporary access code
description: If the Home Hub maps the temporary access code to a named guest, invitation record, phone number, or account, receipt of the code can directly identify who is at the door or who used the code.
assumptions: Assumes the hub or connected backend maintains a mapping from temporary codes to identifiable guest records.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement because the retrieved context did not include the detailed identifiability subtree.

title: Home Hub can detect the guest's presence and arrival time from code entry
description: By receiving and processing the temporary access code, the Home Hub learns that a guest is physically present at the door at a particular time, revealing behavioral and presence information about the guest.
assumptions: Assumes the code is entered in real time at the door and the event is stored or acted upon by the hub.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement because the retrieved context did not include the detailed detectability subtree.

title: Stored code-entry events may reduce the guest's plausible deniability
description: If the Home Hub logs successful or failed temporary-code entries, those records can later be used to claim that a particular guest attempted or obtained entry, limiting their ability to deny the action.
assumptions: Assumes logs are retained and linked to a specific temporary code or guest invitation.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement because the retrieved context did not include the detailed non-repudiation subtree.

title: Guest may lack control over retention and secondary use of code-entry data
description: After the Home Hub receives the temporary access code, the guest may have no practical way to control whether the code-entry event, timestamp, and associated guest identity are stored, shared with other household members, or sent to cloud services.
assumptions: Assumes the hub stores or forwards access events and does not provide the guest with meaningful privacy controls.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement because the retrieved context did not include the detailed non-compliance/control subtree.

title: Excessive retention or over-collection of sensor events in the local log
description: The Local Event Log may store more motion/door/sensor event data than is necessary for the stated purpose, or retain it longer than needed. Because event histories can reveal occupancy patterns, routines, and presence at home, unnecessary storage constitutes avoidable disclosure of personal data at the destination.
assumptions: Assumes the logged events are personal data because they can be linked to household occupants and reveal behavior patterns.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is based on best judgement from LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality concepts; the retrieved context did not provide the exact Dd subtree for this case.

title: Linkability of household behavior across logged sensor events
description: By aggregating motion, door, and other sensor events in one local log, the destination enables linking multiple observations to the same household, device set, time periods, or occupants. This can expose routines such as sleeping, leaving home, or returning, even if single events seem innocuous.
assumptions: Assumes the log preserves timestamps, sensor identifiers, or other stable attributes that allow correlation across entries.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is an informed estimate; the applicability of linkability is strong, but the precise node citation may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Identifiability of occupants from event-log contents
description: The stored event stream may make specific occupants or the household identifiable through combinations of timestamps, sensor locations, device identifiers, and recurring patterns. Even without explicit names, the destination's stored data can single out a home or infer who is present.
assumptions: Assumes event records contain sufficiently granular timestamps and sensor metadata to distinguish a particular household or person.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is approximate; threat applicability depends on the granularity and metadata included in each log entry.

title: Detectability of in-home activity from the existence and timing of log entries
description: The mere presence, frequency, and timing of entries in the Local Event Log can reveal that motion or door activity occurred, allowing an observer with access to the log to detect occupancy or activity without needing full semantic interpretation of each event.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker or unauthorized party can observe log existence, counts, or timestamps.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is approximate; detectability is grounded mainly in metadata and event timing rather than full content access.

title: Unawareness of residents about detailed local event logging
description: Residents may be unaware that the Home Hub writes detailed motion/door/sensor events to a persistent local log, including what is logged, how long it is kept, and who can access it. This undermines transparency and informed expectations about processing at the destination.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not clearly notify users about local logging behavior, retention, and access controls.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is approximate; unawareness depends on the product's notice and configuration UX.

title: Logging may exceed consent or user privacy preferences
description: If users did not explicitly consent to persistent storage of detailed sensor events, or if the log continues despite privacy settings that imply reduced monitoring, the destination's storage can violate consent and choice expectations.
assumptions: Assumes consent, legitimate-basis constraints, or privacy preferences apply to local event logging and may not be enforced by the datastore behavior.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is approximate and applicability depends on the system's consent model and jurisdictional requirements.

title: Lack of accountability over who caused or accessed logged events
description: If the Local Event Log does not preserve trustworthy provenance and access records, occupants may be unable to prove whether specific entries were generated, altered, or viewed, weakening accountability for privacy-relevant processing of sensor data.
assumptions: Assumes the datastore lacks tamper-evident auditability or provenance metadata for writes and reads.
uncertainty_note: Non-repudiation is less directly evidenced by the short flow description than other threats; included because accountability gaps around event logging are plausible but context-dependent.

title: Uploading identifiable home video to cloud enables direct identification of residents and visitors
description: The Home Hub sends recorded camera clips that can contain faces, voices, interiors, timestamps, and other directly identifying content to cloud storage. The act of disclosing these clips to another system increases the risk that natural persons captured in the footage are identified.
assumptions: Recorded clips contain personal data such as recognizable people, voices, or uniquely identifying home context.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement; exact sub-node may vary depending on the project's threat-tree version.

title: Upload traffic metadata can link clips to a specific household and behavior patterns
description: Even aside from clip contents, the upload flow can expose metadata such as device identifiers, account identifiers, IP address, upload timing, clip frequency, and file sizes. This metadata can be used to link multiple uploads to the same household and infer occupancy or activity patterns.
assumptions: Network or application-layer metadata is observable or retained by intermediaries or the receiving service.
uncertainty_note: Exact applicable sub-node for linkability depends on the threat-tree granularity available in the project.

title: Upload metadata may allow inference of presence, routines, or incidents
description: The cadence, timing, duration, and size of uploaded clips may reveal when motion occurred, when occupants are home or away, and whether unusual events happened, even without viewing the clip contents.
assumptions: Clip uploads are event-driven or otherwise correlated with household activity.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgement because the retrieved context did not include inference sub-nodes.

title: Cloud storage can identify individuals from stored video content
description: Once clips are received and stored, the cloud video storage environment can process or expose footage in ways that identify residents, visitors, neighbors, or passers-by captured in the recordings.
assumptions: Stored clips remain accessible to cloud-side services, administrators, or integrated analytics beyond the originating device.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node may differ by threat-tree version.

title: Stored clips enable inference about private life inside and around the home
description: Analysis of uploaded footage can reveal routines, relationships, possessions, health indicators, religious practices, children's presence, and other sensitive facts not explicitly provided by the user.
assumptions: Cloud-side storage or associated services permit viewing, indexing, or analysis of clip contents and metadata.
uncertainty_note: Inference is strongly plausible for home video, but the exact threat-tree sub-node is approximate.

title: Cloud retention and secondary access can disclose sensitive home video
description: Receiving and storing clips in the cloud creates a risk that footage is disclosed to unauthorized internal staff, external attackers, third parties, or through misconfiguration, exposing intimate details of the household.
assumptions: Cloud storage is reachable by multiple components or personnel, or may be subject to breach/misconfiguration.
uncertainty_note: Specific disclosure sub-node is approximate without the full threat-tree excerpt.

title: Cloud video storage may retain clips longer than necessary
description: The destination data store may keep uploaded camera clips beyond the period necessary for the stated purpose, violating storage limitation obligations and increasing privacy risk.
assumptions: Retention periods are not strictly minimized, enforced, or communicated to data subjects.

title: Data subjects may be unaware that home camera footage is uploaded to cloud storage
description: Residents, visitors, neighbors, or passers-by captured by the camera may not understand that recordings are transferred off-device to a cloud data store, reducing transparency about processing and storage.
assumptions: Notice is limited or absent for all individuals who may be recorded.
uncertainty_note: Exact unawareness sub-node is approximate.

title: The upload action may be insufficiently provable or attributable
description: If the Home Hub does not create reliable audit evidence for clip uploads, it may be difficult to prove what footage was uploaded, when, and under whose configuration or authority. This can hinder accountability for privacy-relevant disclosures.
assumptions: Audit logging, integrity protection, or user-visible upload records may be incomplete.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation applicability depends on whether accountability for uploads is in scope; included with moderate confidence.

title: Home Hub shares more motion-alert data than necessary
description: The Home Hub may forward a real-time motion alert containing excessive personal data to the backend, such as precise timestamps, device identifiers, household identifiers, sensor metadata, or contextual details beyond what is needed to notify the user. Because motion events reveal occupancy and behavior patterns, unnecessary fields increase avoidable disclosure.
assumptions: Assumes the alert payload can include metadata beyond the minimum needed to deliver the notification.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-judgement based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimization structure; exact node label may differ in the canonical tree.

title: Motion-alert traffic can identify the household or device in transit
description: Identifiers or quasi-identifiers carried on the flow, such as hub ID, account ID, IP address, routing metadata, or stable protocol identifiers, may allow an observer of the transmission to identify the specific household or resident associated with the motion alert.
assumptions: Assumes network or application-layer metadata is observable to some party on the path or at network boundaries.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node id is approximate; the applicability of in-transit identification depends on transport protections and metadata exposure.

title: Repeated motion alerts are linkable over time
description: Even if payload contents are limited, repeated real-time alerts with stable identifiers, consistent endpoints, or recognizable timing patterns can be linked together to build a profile of activity at the same home. This enables inference of routines such as occupancy, sleep, or absence patterns.
assumptions: Assumes alerts recur over time and contain stable metadata or observable timing characteristics.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; linkage may arise from metadata and timing rather than explicit identifiers alone.

title: Motion-alert timing enables detection of resident activity
description: The mere presence and timing of real-time motion-alert transmissions can allow an observer to detect that someone is moving in the home at specific moments, even without reading full payload contents. This reveals sensitive behavioral events through traffic analysis.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker or third party can observe traffic timing, frequency, or volume on the path.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is best-judgement; this is a classic detectability-via-traffic-analysis scenario.

title: Backend stores or further disseminates motion alerts beyond notification needs
description: On receipt, the mobile app backend may retain, enrich, or share motion-alert data for analytics, troubleshooting, profiling, or onward delivery beyond what is strictly required to notify the user. Because motion alerts expose in-home activity, unnecessary backend processing or retention creates avoidable disclosure risk.
assumptions: Assumes the backend persists or reuses received alerts beyond transient delivery.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; exact canonical node for recipient-side storage/sharing may differ.

title: Backend can link motion alerts with other user data
description: The backend can correlate incoming motion alerts with account records, device inventories, app usage, location history, or other telemetry already held about the user. This may create a richer profile of household behavior than users expect.
assumptions: Assumes the backend has access to other datasets keyed by account, device, or household.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; linkage at the destination depends on broader backend data holdings.

title: Backend can identify residents from motion-alert data
description: By combining the alert with account and device records, the backend may identify the household or specific user associated with the motion event. If multiple residents share the system, backend-side enrichment may narrow the event to a particular person or role.
assumptions: Assumes the backend maintains subscriber/account mappings and possibly user profiles.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; identification of a specific individual may depend on available account context.

title: Users may be unaware that raw motion events are sent to the backend in real time
description: If the system does not clearly communicate that the Home Hub forwards motion alerts to a backend service, users may lack awareness of this collection and transfer of in-home activity data. This undermines transparency about how sensor events leave the local environment.
assumptions: Assumes notices or UI explanations do not clearly describe this real-time backend transmission.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; unawareness depends on the quality of notices and product UX.

title: Backend processing of motion alerts may exceed or conflict with user consent
description: If users consent only to core alerting, but the backend also uses motion-alert data for analytics, model training, service improvement, or sharing with partners, the processing may not align with the scope of consent or user choice.
assumptions: Assumes consent is required for some secondary uses and that such uses may occur or be enabled by design.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; applicability depends on the system's consent model and actual downstream uses.

title: Notification reveals more personal data than necessary
description: The backend may include excessive detail in the motion alert (e.g., exact timestamp, camera/location name, image snapshot, or inferred occupancy status) when only a minimal alert is needed. This constitutes avoidable disclosure of personal data to the homeowner's device.
assumptions: The push notification content can contain personal/contextual details beyond a generic alert.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality concepts; exact subnode may differ in the canonical tree.

title: Push-notification metadata discloses sensitive context in transit
description: Even if notification payload is limited, metadata on the flow—such as recipient identifier, delivery timing, frequency of motion alerts, or notification headers via push infrastructure—can reveal occupancy patterns, routines, or that the household uses a security system.
assumptions: The notification traverses third-party push infrastructure or networks where metadata is observable or processable.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; threat is grounded in implicit disclosure via metadata.

title: Notification content may be exposed on the homeowner's device lock screen
description: On receipt, the phone may display the motion-detected notification on the lock screen or wearable companion, allowing bystanders or other device users to learn that motion occurred, infer presence/absence patterns, or see location-specific details.
assumptions: The homeowner's device is configured to show notification previews or is accessible to others nearby.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort; destination-side disclosure via device display is the key concern.

title: Repeated alerts enable linkage of household activity over time
description: A series of motion notifications on this flow can be correlated over time to link events to the same household/device, building a profile of routines, occupancy, and behavior patterns.
assumptions: An observer of the flow or push service can correlate repeated notifications to the same recipient/account/device.
uncertainty_note: Applicable linkage threat is clear, but exact subnode id is approximate.

title: Notification metadata can identify the homeowner or household
description: Identifiers used to route the push notification (device token, account identifier, endpoint metadata) may directly or indirectly identify the homeowner or uniquely single out their household.
assumptions: Routing or push-service metadata is accessible to infrastructure providers or attackers with network visibility.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; identification via routing metadata is the substantive threat.

title: Sharing analytics may enable cross-context linkage by the vendor
description: Even if described as aggregated device-usage analytics, the backend's act of sending recurring analytics datasets to the same cloud analytics vendor can allow records about the same app population, tenant, cohort, or device segment to be linked across reporting periods or with other datasets already held by the vendor.
assumptions: Assumes the payload contains stable cohort keys, app/account identifiers, timestamps, campaign identifiers, or sufficiently granular dimensions that permit correlation over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement because the retrieved context confirms applicability of Linkability for Process->ExternalEntity but does not provide the detailed threat-tree node list.

title: Aggregated analytics may still disclose information about individuals or small groups
description: The backend may disclose personal or sensitive information if the shared analytics are only nominally aggregated: small cell counts, rare event combinations, fine-grained timestamps, location/device attributes, or segmentation dimensions can allow singling out or inference about individuals or very small groups.
assumptions: Assumes aggregation thresholds, k-anonymity-style controls, suppression, or noise injection are absent or weak.
uncertainty_note: Node id is approximate; exact LINDDUN Pro subtree for disclosure is not present in the retrieved snippets.

title: Flow metadata can identify the app operator or analytics relationship
description: Even if payload contents are protected, the existence of a regular data flow from the mobile app backend to a specific analytics vendor can reveal identifying information about the app operator, service usage, business relationships, or deployment environment through network metadata such as endpoints, DNS names, certificates, timing, and volume.
assumptions: Assumes observers can access network metadata or service-routing information.
uncertainty_note: This is a data-flow-centric identifiability threat based on metadata in transit; exact node id is best-judgement.

title: Vendor can link received analytics with other customer or platform data
description: At receipt, the cloud analytics vendor may combine the analytics with other datasets it controls, enabling linkage across customers, apps, SDK telemetry, advertising identifiers, or historical submissions. This can increase the ability to correlate behavior patterns beyond the original purpose of the transfer.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor has additional datasets or platform-wide telemetry and contractual/technical separation is limited.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree citation is approximate.

title: Vendor may identify users or devices from supposedly aggregated analytics
description: The recipient may be able to identify a user, device, household, or small cohort by combining the received analytics with auxiliary information, especially where aggregates are granular, longitudinal, or segmented by uncommon attributes.
assumptions: Assumes auxiliary data is available to the vendor and the aggregation level is not sufficiently protective.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; applicability is strong if aggregation is coarse only in name.

title: Recipient-side analysis may disclose more than intended
description: Once received, the analytics vendor can derive additional insights about user behavior, device populations, or sensitive usage patterns that exceed what the sender intended to reveal, creating disclosure through enrichment, segmentation, or downstream reporting.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor is permitted or technically able to perform enrichment or secondary analytics.
uncertainty_note: Node id is best-judgement due to missing detailed tree mapping in context.

title: Secondary analytics use may exceed users' expectations
description: Using backend-shared device-usage analytics for the vendor's own product improvement, benchmarking, advertising, model training, or other secondary purposes may be unexpected from the users' perspective, especially if they only expected analytics for the app operator's service improvement.
assumptions: Assumes notices/consent do not clearly cover the vendor's downstream or secondary uses.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro subtree id for Unawareness is approximate.

title: Transfer to analytics vendor may be non-compliant with data-minimization or third-party transfer rules
description: If the shared analytics remain personal data, or can reasonably be re-identified, sending them to the cloud analytics vendor may violate applicable privacy requirements unless there is a valid legal basis, appropriate processor/controller allocation, contractual safeguards, cross-border transfer controls, retention limits, and minimization measures.
assumptions: Assumes relevant privacy law or contractual obligations apply and governance controls may be incomplete.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends heavily on jurisdiction, contracts, and whether the data is truly anonymized.

title: Linkability via retrieval metadata on the video-fetch flow
description: Metadata on the retrieval flow (e.g., clip identifier, camera/home identifier, account/session identifier, timestamps, IP/device identifiers, request frequency) can allow an observer or intermediary with access to the transmission context to correlate multiple playback requests to the same homeowner, household, camera, or event history.
assumptions: Applies if the flow exposes stable identifiers or observable metadata beyond what is strictly necessary, or if network/intermediary logs are accessible.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is approximate; exact LINDDUN Pro subnode for linkability of communication metadata was not provided in the retrieved context.

title: Identifiability of homeowner or household from video retrieval traffic
description: The content or metadata of the video retrieval flow may directly or indirectly identify the homeowner or household, for example through account tokens, camera identifiers, precise timestamps, network identifiers, or clip URLs that embed personal identifiers.
assumptions: Applies if identifiers are present in transit or inferable from request structure, headers, URLs, or associated logs.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is approximate; exact identifiability subnode for data-in-transit metadata was not included in the retrieved context.

title: Backend learns sensitive inferences from requested video clips
description: By receiving and processing requests for specific stored clips, the mobile app backend can infer sensitive information about the homeowner's behavior, routines, occupancy, visitors, or incidents captured by the video, beyond merely serving playback.
assumptions: Applies if clip selection, timestamps, camera location, or playback patterns are logged, profiled, or otherwise analyzed by the backend.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro detectability/disclosure subnode is approximate; this threat is grounded in inference from received personal data at the destination.

title: Backend can disclose video content or playback history beyond intended recipients
description: Once the backend retrieves the stored clip, improper access control, excessive internal access, insecure temporary storage, or verbose logging could expose the video content or the fact that a homeowner viewed a particular clip to unauthorized parties.
assumptions: Applies if the backend stores, caches, logs, or redistributes retrieved clips or playback events.
uncertainty_note: Exact disclosure subnode is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the relevant Dd subtree.

title: Secondary use of retrieved video or playback telemetry
description: The backend may use retrieved video clips or associated playback telemetry for purposes beyond homeowner playback, such as analytics, model training, employee review, product improvement, or law-enforcement sharing, without a compatible legal basis or user expectation.
assumptions: Applies if backend processing extends beyond the immediate playback purpose.
uncertainty_note: Exact unawareness subnode is approximate; the retrieved context did not provide the U subtree.

title: Storage limitation violation for retrieved clips or playback logs
description: The backend may retain fetched video clips, temporary caches, derived thumbnails, or playback/access logs longer than necessary for the playback purpose, violating storage limitation obligations.
assumptions: Applies if P2 persists retrieved content or related logs without strict retention limits.
